title: Product topology and open rectangles
terms: product topology; open rectangle; coordinate projection.

exposition.text:
The product topology on X × Y has basis U × V , with U, V open in their respective factors.
For finitely many Euclidean factors this agrees with the usual Euclidean topology. Coordinate
projections are continuous and open. A map into a product is continuous exactly when its
coordinate maps are continuous.
2
For nonempty factors, closure satisfies A × B = A × B. A thin subset such as a line in R may
be closed but has empty interior. Openness in the plane requires a full small rectangle or disk,
not just openness along a curve.
Open coordinate projections of a subset do not by themselves make that subset open. Although
projection need not send closed sets to closed sets in general, projection X × K → X is a
closed map when K is compact: a finite cover of the omitted fiber supplies one neighborhood
missing the projection. The topology on each factor also matters when checking continuity of
coordinate maps.

question.text:
2
Let A = (Q ∩ [0, 1]) × (0, 1) in R . What is its boundary?
2
(A) The four edges of [0, 1] .
2
(B) [0, 1]
(C) {0, 1} × [0, 1]
(D) A
(E) ∅

solution.text:
2
The closure is [0, 1] , since rational first coordinates are dense. The interior is empty be-
cause every open rectangle contains an irrational first coordinate. Therefore the entire
closed square is the boundary.

question.text:
2
Let π : R → R be π(x, y) = x. Which statement is false?
(A) π is continuous.
(B) π maps open sets to open sets.
(C) π maps compact sets to compact sets.
(D) π maps every closed set to a closed set.
(E) π maps connected sets to connected sets.

solution.text:
The closed hyperbola xy = 1 projects to R \ {0}, which is not closed. Continuity gives preser-
vation of compactness and connectedness; products of intervals show projections are open.

question.text:
The codomain Y is R × R with the usual topology in the first factor and the discrete topology in
the second. Which maps from the usual real line into Y are continuous?
I. t 7→ (t, t).
II. t 7→ (t, 0).
III. t 7→ (0, ⌊t⌋).
(A) I only (B) II only (C) I and II only (D) II and III only (E) All three

solution.text:
A map into a product is continuous exactly when each coordinate map into its stated factor
is continuous. The second coordinate of I has singleton preimages, which are not open in
the usual line. For III, the preimage of {0} in the second factor is [0, 1), again not open. II
has a continuous first coordinate and a constant second coordinate.

question.text:
2
Let S = {(x, y) ∈ R : xy = 0}. Which description is correct?
(A) S is open because both coordinate projections are open subsets of R.
(B) S is closed with empty interior, although both coordinate projections equal R.
(C) S has nonempty interior only at the origin.
(D) S is neither open nor closed.
(E) S is compact.

solution.text:
S is the inverse image of the closed set {0} under the continuous function (x, y) 7→ xy, so
it is closed. Every disk contains a point with both coordinates nonzero, so the interior is
empty. Its projections are each the whole real line, illustrating that open projections do not
imply that the original subset is open. It is unbounded and hence not compact.

question.text:
Let C be a closed subset of R × [0, 1] with the product topology. Which statement about its
first-coordinate projection π(C) must hold?
(A) It is compact.
(B) It is open.
(C) It is closed, but need not be bounded.
(D) It is an interval.
(E) It is all of R unless C is empty.

solution.text:
If x ∈/ π(C), the entire compact fiber {x} × [0, 1] lies in the open complement of C. Each
fiber point has a product neighborhood avoiding C. Finitely many second-coordinate
neighborhoods cover [0, 1]; intersect their first-coordinate neighborhoods to obtain a neigh-
borhood of x avoiding π(C). Thus the projection is closed. Taking C = R × {0} shows
boundedness need not follow.
